content: Conjugated bile salts can accumulate in the liver, leading to clinical symptoms. If concurrent use of medications affecting bile salt metabolism is necessary, it is essential to monitor serum transaminases and bilirubin levels closely. Cholestyramine reduces the levels or effects of cholic acid by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract. To minimize interaction, cholic acid should be taken at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after bile acid-binding resins. Close monitoring is advised. Clarithromycin increases the toxicity of cholic acid by reducing its elimination. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. Avoid using inhibitors of the bile salt export pump (BSEP), as they may worsen the accumulation of conjugated bile salts in the liver, potentially causing clinical symptoms. Colesevelam decreases the levels or effects of cholic acid through drug binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Caution is advised, and monitoring is necessary. Cholic acid should be taken at least 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after bile acid-binding resins. Colestipol also reduces the levels or effects of cholic acid by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract. Similar precautions as with colesevelam should be followed. Cyclosporine increases the toxicity of cholic acid by decreasing its elimination. Therapy adjustments and close monitoring are required. Avoid BSEP inhibitors to prevent exacerbation of bile salt accumulation in the liver. Dipyridamole increases cholic acid toxicity by reducing its elimination. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is necessary. Avoid BSEP inhibitors for the same reasons as above. Eluxadoline increases cholic acid levels by decreasing its metabolism and may also increase systemic exposure to co-administered OATP1B1 substrates. Use caution and monitor closely. Adverse effects of cholic acid therapy include diarrhea (2%), reflux esophagitis (1%), malaise (1%), jaundice (1%), skin lesions (1%), nausea (1%), abdominal pain (1%), intestinal polyps (1%), urinary tract infections (1%), and peripheral neuropathy (1%). Gastrointestinal disorders such as discomfort, distension, emesis, and constipation have also been reported. General disorders include fever, while skin-related issues include rash. Liver function may worsen, and exacerbation of liver impairment has been observed. Liver function should be monitored regularly, and therapy should be discontinued if clinical or laboratory indicators of worsening liver function or cholestasis are observed. Concurrent elevations of GGT and ALT may indicate overdose, necessitating discontinuation of therapy. Severe hepatotoxicity has been reported in patients with cirrhosis following post-market use of cholic acid therapy. The possibility of liver impairment exacerbation in these patients cannot be ruled out. No studies have been conducted in pregnant women or animals to assess the safety of cholic acid. Limited case reports suggest healthy outcomes in infants born to women taking cholic acid for 3β-HSD deficiency. Endogenous cholic acid is present in human milk, but the effects on breastfed infants or milk production are unknown. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and potential adverse effects on the infant. In cases of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., call 911 for severe symptoms or contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Do not dispose of medications improperly; follow proper disposal guidelines.
